title: FinOps for LLMs — Unit Economics and Multi-Tenant Attribution

questions.question: Why does traditional FinOps break on LLM spend?
options: LLMs don't cost money, since the lesson treats token spend as effectively free at typical volumes
Costs are token-transactions rather than resource-uptime; tags don't auto-propagate from API calls and you must stamp user/task/tenant at the call site
LLM bills are always free under a fixed monthly quota that every provider grants by default
Cloud providers refuse to itemize LLM spend at all, leaving teams with only a single lump-sum invoice
questions.explanation: The lesson states LLM costs are token-transactions rather than resource-uptime, so cloud-style tags do not auto-propagate from an API call the way they do for EC2 or S3 -- you must stamp user/task/tenant metadata at the call site yourself.

questions.question: Which three attribution dimensions does the lesson require instrumenting on day one?
options: Provider, model, API version — a vendor-tracking triple, not the lesson's three attribution dimensions
Region, AZ, datacenter — an infrastructure-location triple, not the lesson's three attribution dimensions
GPU, CPU, RAM — a hardware-resource triple, not the lesson's three attribution dimensions
Per-user (user_id), per-task (task_id + route), per-tenant (tenant_id)
questions.explanation: The lesson's three attribution dimensions are per-user (user_id, for seat pricing and expansion), per-task (task_id + route, for product-surface cost), and per-tenant (tenant_id, for unit economics and renewal) -- instrumented at the call site from day one.

questions.question: Which four token layers should be broken out in cost attribution?
options: Input, output, network, disk — infrastructure-transfer terms, not the lesson's four token layers
Cache, model, gateway, observability — infra components, not the lesson's four token layers
Prompt, tool, memory, response
GPU, CPU, RAM, storage — hardware resources, not the lesson's four token layers
questions.explanation: The lesson breaks token spend into prompt, tool, memory, and response layers, noting that bucketing all four together makes cost optimization blind to which layer is actually driving spend.

questions.question: What is the kill-switch trigger in the enforcement ladder?
options: Tenant spend z-score > 4 relative to baseline; auto-pause tenant and page on-call
Latency P50 > 2s, a performance threshold rather than the spend-anomaly trigger the lesson defines
Any 5xx response, treating a single server error as grounds for an automatic tenant pause
Spend over $1 in a minute, a flat dollar threshold rather than the z-score the lesson defines
questions.explanation: The lesson's third rung of the enforcement ladder triggers when a tenant's spend z-score exceeds 4 relative to its own baseline, auto-pausing the tenant and paging on-call, escalating to ops and customer success.

questions.question: Which unit metric does the lesson recommend instead of $/M tokens?
options: Cost per gateway, aggregating spend by which gateway instance routed the request
Cost per product outcome (e.g. cost per resolved support ticket, cost per generated article, cost per successful agent task)
Cost per GPU-hour, tying spend to the underlying hardware rather than a product outcome
Cost per second, a raw time-based metric rather than the outcome-based one the lesson recommends
questions.explanation: The lesson calls $/M tokens 'vendor speak' and recommends tying cost to a product outcome instead -- cost per resolved support ticket, cost per generated article, cost per successful agent task -- so optimization has an anchor.

questions.question: Which attribution pattern does the lesson call the highest-accuracy one mature teams use?
options: Sampling and extrapolation, sampling 5-10% of traffic and multiplying — cost-effective but misses tails
Model-based allocation, a regression-based estimate used mainly for legacy data without tags
Tag-and-aggregate only, simple and rough, but not the pattern the lesson calls highest-accuracy
Telemetry joiner — join traces to billing via trace IDs
questions.explanation: The lesson names the telemetry-joiner pattern -- joining traces to billing via trace IDs -- as the highest-accuracy attribution pattern and what mature teams do, versus the simpler and rougher tag-and-aggregate approach.
